summary: Defines the Eifel response algorithm, which lets a TCP sender respond to a detected spurious timeout. It adapts the retransmission timer to avoid further spurious timeouts and can avoid unneeded go-back-N retransmission.

plainLanguage.summary: When you wrongly think your letter got lost and send it again, this helps you realize and stop wasting effort.

questions: what is the eifel response algorithm
what is a spurious timeout in tcp
how does tcp recover from a spurious timeout
what does eifel do to the retransmission timer
subtitle: How a TCP sender should undo the damage after it discovers a retransmission timeout was a false alarm.

tldr.problem: A TCP sender sometimes retransmits after a timeout even though nothing was lost, because the delay was only a temporary spike. The sender then needlessly resends data and slashes its sending rate.
tldr.mechanism: Once a separate detection algorithm says the timeout was spurious, the Eifel response algorithm resumes sending new data, restores the saved congestion control state, and makes the retransmission timer more conservative.
tldr.outcome: The sender avoids unnecessary go-back-N retransmits and packet bursts, and is less likely to time out spuriously again. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 4015 is a Proposed Standard from February 2005, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Eifel Response Does
sections.content:
The Eifel response algorithm lets a TCP sender react to a spurious timeout: a retransmission timeout that fired even though the original data was not lost. It does not detect the problem itself. It relies on a detection algorithm such as the Eifel detection algorithm from RFC 3522.

When a spurious timeout is detected, the response does three things. It adapts the retransmission timer to avoid further spurious timeouts, it can avoid the often unnecessary go-back-N retransmits (depending on the detection algorithm), and it restores the congestion control state so that packet bursts are avoided.

A note in the RFC explains that an earlier version also covered spurious fast retransmits. That part was removed for the time being because no consensus was reached on how to adapt the duplicate acknowledgement threshold.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP sometimes thinks a packet got lost when it was only slow. This algorithm is the plan for what to do once TCP finds out it was wrong.

sections.title: Pairing with a Detection Algorithm
sections.content:
If the Eifel response algorithm is implemented, it MUST be implemented together with a detection algorithm that is specified in a standards track or experimental RFC.

Detection algorithms communicate through the variable SpuriousRecovery, with the values and meaning defined in RFC 3522. This RFC adds one more constant, LATE_SPUR_TO, set equal to -1. A detection algorithm sets it when the spurious retransmit is detected from the ACK for the retransmit, as opposed to an ACK for an original transmit. Detection based on the DSACK option from RFC 3708 is the example given.
sections.plainLanguage: The response only knows what to do if someone else first tells it, "that was a false alarm." That helper is the detection algorithm.

sections.title: The Algorithm Step by Step
sections.content:
A TCP sender that has a suitable detection algorithm enabled MAY use the response. The steps MUST be taken only when a timeout-based loss recovery starts, that is, when the first timeout-based retransmit is sent. The algorithm MUST NOT be restarted while that recovery is still in progress, for example on later timeouts for the same segment.

  • Step 0: before cwnd and ssthresh change, save pipe_prev as the larger of FlightSize and ssthresh. Also save SRTT_prev as SRTT + (2 * G) and RTTVAR_prev as RTTVAR.
  • DET: the detection algorithm runs and sets SpuriousRecovery.
  • Step 7: if the value is SPUR_TO, go to step 8. If it is LATE_SPUR_TO, go to step 9. Otherwise stop.
  • Step 8: set SND.NXT to SND.MAX.
  • Step 9: reverse the congestion control state, unless the acceptable ACK has the ECN-Echo flag set.
  • Step 10: if congestion window validation is implemented, set T_last to tcpnow.
  • Step 11: adapt the retransmission timer on the first RTT sample taken from new data.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a short checklist: remember how fast you were going, wait for the "false alarm" news, then go back to sending new stuff, restore your speed safely, and be more patient with your timer.

sections.title: Skipping Needless go-back-N Retransmits
sections.content:
Without the TCP timestamps option, the sender suffers from the retransmission ambiguity problem. When the first acceptable ACK arrives after a spurious timeout, the sender must assume it answers the retransmit, and must assume all other outstanding segments were lost. So SND.NXT ends up equal to SND.UNA, which is what causes the often unnecessary go-back-N retransmits.

During that phase the sender breaks packet conservation. Because the retransmits are sent during slow-start, for each original transmit leaving the network two retransmits are sent into it, as long as SND.NXT does not equal SND.MAX.

Once the spurious timeout is detected from an ACK for an original transmit, it is safe to resume with previously unsent data. Step 8 does this by setting SND.NXT to SND.MAX. It runs only when SpuriousRecovery equals SPUR_TO.
sections.plainLanguage: If you think everything was lost, you resend it all. But if it was just slow, you are sending copies of letters that already arrived. Step 8 says, "skip the copies and carry on with new letters."

sections.title: Restoring the Congestion State and the Timer
sections.content:
Entering loss recovery reduces cwnd and ssthresh. If the loss recovery turns out to be false, the reduction was unnecessary. In step 9, unless the acceptable ACK carries the ECN-Echo flag (in which case the sender MUST NOT reverse the state), cwnd is set to FlightSize + min(bytes_acked, IW) and ssthresh is set to pipe_prev. The initial window IW caps the burst, since it is an acceptable burst size for a yet unprobed network.

Step 10 resets T_last so that Congestion Window Validation (RFC 2861) does not mistake a delay spike for an idle period.

Step 11 adapts the timer on the first RTT sample from previously unsent data, when the timer follows RFC 2988: SRTT becomes max(SRTT_prev, RTT-SAMPLE), RTTVAR becomes max(RTTVAR_prev, RTT-SAMPLE/2), and RTO becomes SRTT + max(G, 4*RTTVAR). The bounds check is run and the timer restarted. The extra 2 * G is described as a reasonable upper bound on a timer firing "a tad too early".
sections.plainLanguage: TCP slowed down because it was scared, so now it carefully speeds back up to where it was, but not in one giant rush. It also sets its waiting timer a little longer so it is not fooled again.

sections.title: Advanced Loss Recovery Is Crucial
sections.content:
The authors studied environments where spurious timeouts and multiple losses from the same flight of packets often coincide. In those cases, running the response without an advanced loss recovery scheme such as the SACK-based scheme of RFC 3517 or NewReno (RFC 3782) hurts end-to-end performance, because the more conservative sender is often forced into another timeout. The RFC therefore recommends always running it together with one of those two schemes. Limited Transmit and Early Retransmit add robustness.

With NewReno, step 1 of NewReno SHOULD be modified, but only if SpuriousRecovery equals SPUR_TO: on the third duplicate ACK outside Fast Recovery, go to step 1A. Step 1B becomes obsolete because step 8 avoids the duplicate ACKs that unnecessary go-back-N retransmits would cause.
sections.plainLanguage: If several letters are really lost at once, a careful sender needs a good recovery trick, or it will end up waiting and timing out again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A detection algorithm could be fooled by spoofed ACKs that make genuine retransmits look spurious. If that happens together with the Eifel response, congestion control could effectively be disabled at the sender.

Should this be a concern, the response SHOULD only be run with detection algorithms known to be safe against such ACK spoofing attacks. The RFC gives the safe variant of the Eifel detection algorithm in RFC 3522 as a reliable method to protect against this risk.
sections.plainLanguage: A trickster could send fake "false alarm" messages so TCP wrongly speeds up. So TCP should only trust detectors that are hard to fool.

viz.caption: THE STEPS OF THE RESPONSE ALGORITHM (RFC 4015)

items.label: Save state
items.desc: Store pipe_prev, SRTT_prev and RTTVAR_prev before cwnd and ssthresh change.

items.label: Resume new data
items.desc: Set SND.NXT to SND.MAX when SpuriousRecovery is SPUR_TO.

items.label: Reverse congestion state
items.desc: Set cwnd and ssthresh back, unless ECN-Echo is set.

items.label: Adapt timer
items.desc: Make the retransmission timer more conservative on the first RTT sample from new data.
